checkpoints.title: Tradeoff duel
checkpoints.prompt: Last-second bidding flurry. How is bid order decided?

options.label: Compare against the cached max bid
options.verdict: Two bids read the same max, both conclude they are highest, and both write. The read-modify-write is not atomic, so under exactly the burst the product is designed for, you accept a losing bid.

options.label: Atomic conditional write
options.verdict: Make the database or a Lua script do the comparison in the same operation as the write. A losing bid fails atomically and is told so, rather than silently overwriting a higher one.

defend.prompt: What else does the auction close need?

options.label: A server-side clock, not the client's
The close boundary evaluated atomically with the bid
An append-only bid log for dispute resolution
Bids rejected once the client's timer hits zero

defend.explain: Client clocks are unreliable and trivially manipulated. The server decides both the ordering and whether the auction was still open, in the same atomic step that accepts the bid.

checkpoints.title: Capacity ladder
checkpoints.prompt: A closing auction with a last-second flurry.

rungs.note: Under ~200ms end to end, or the final seconds feel broken.

rungs.q: Whose clock decides whether bidding is open
rungs.note: Always the server, evaluated inside the same atomic operation.

rungs.q: What viewers need during the flurry
rungs.note: Price updates can be coalesced; the accepted bid cannot.

checkpoints.explain: The write path must be strictly correct; the broadcast path only needs to be fast and roughly current. Separating those two is the whole design.

checkpoints.title: Architecture builder
checkpoints.explain: The Lua script decides acceptance and close-time in one atomic step, the bid log makes it durable and auditable, then pub/sub fans the new price to viewers. Broadcast happens after durability — never before, or you can show a price that was never accepted.

checkpoints.title: Spot the bottleneck
checkpoints.prompt: The winning bid was recorded 3 seconds after the auction closed.
checkpoints.explain: Every component is fast, so nothing was queued — the close boundary itself was evaluated against the wrong time. One node's clock drifted 3.2 seconds, so it accepted a bid it should have rejected. Auction close is a time-based correctness boundary, which makes clock discipline part of the design rather than an operational detail.

wrong.Redis Lua CAS: The compare-and-set worked exactly as written — against a bad timestamp.
wrong.Bid Log: It durably recorded a bid that should never have been accepted.
wrong.Bid Service: Healthy latency. The ordering logic ran correctly on incorrect input.
